en: The Sūtra on Slandering the Buddha, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha.
In the midst [of the assembly], he was together with a great community of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus and eighty thousand bodhisattvas.
At that time, there was in the assembly a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Vigataśokā, seated in the great gathering,
along with the bodhisattva mahāsattva Siṃhavikrīḍita, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Jñānaprabha, and others.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Brahmameghasvaranirghoṣa, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sukṛtakuśaladharmaratnapuṣpāvabhāsa,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Siṃhavikrāntagāmīmeghastanita-ghoṣa, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Prabhāsavikramayaśas, and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Anantajñānaskandhavicintitavyūha.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas— the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Anantaratnakusumanāman,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Prajñāprabhāpratibhānavyākaraṇamati, and these ten Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas—
were assembled and seated in the assembly; for seven years they had diligently practiced the dhāraṇī, yet they were unable to attain it.
When the seven years had passed, he became filled with sorrow; his mind was still not settled, let alone regarding the dhāraṇī.

Failing to obtain what he sought, weariness arose in his heart. Having remained free from the shroud of delusion for seven years, he constantly practiced walking meditation seeking the dhāraṇī but could not attain it.
He then abandoned the precepts and returned home, distancing himself from the Buddha-dharma and becoming base.
Those of inferior conduct give rise to doubt and confusion within the Buddha-dharma;
such are their faults. King Ajātaśatru was seated in a great assembly.

At that time, the World-Honored One had already severed his doubts and regrets. Having thus eliminated his doubts and regrets, Ajātaśatru attained liberation from all distress and affliction. Over the course of seven days, he renounced his wealth in great charity. When this great giving was completed after the seven days, seven hundred million sentient beings gathered together at the Buddha’s dwelling for the sake of hearing the Dharma.
Those ten bodhisattvas, sons of good family, who had already incurred offenses within the Buddha-dharma were also seated in the assembly.

At that time, there was in the assembly a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Abhayacārin (Fearless Practice), who had attained dhāraṇī, perfected the dharma-patience (*dharmakṣānti*) over incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), and had attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Possessing various forms of eloquence (*pratibhāna*), he was able to know the gateway to the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*), was able to expound the Dharma-gateways, and was able to discern the profound inclinations and faith-understandings of sentient beings in order to preach the Dharma for them.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Abhayacārin rose from his seat, adjusted his robe to expose one shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said:
"O Virtuous One!

Within this assembly, there are ten virtuous men who have diligently practiced the dhāraṇīs for seven years; yet, as their aspirations were not fulfilled, they abandoned the Buddha-dharma and returned to lay life.
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
As you have explained through skillful means, this son of good family will quickly come to understand.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Abhayacaryā, saying:

“Good son! You should know that these ten good sons have never before heard the Dharma-gate of slandering the Buddha. These good sons have previously slandered the Buddha; for this reason, they are unable to swiftly attain supernormal powers.”
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Abhayacārin addressed the Tathāgata in verse, saying:
"I now ask you, O Benevolent One, O King of Dharma of Radiant Light:
If one practices the conduct of a bodhisattva, how are evil karmas purified?"
The name of immeasurable, supreme wisdom, The unobstructed wisdom of the ten powers, Liberation free from conceptual proliferation— You have spoken of the pure conduct of bodhisattvas.
I ask about immeasurable wisdom; I ask about the severing of evil intent.
I ask the Peerless Honored One: What is the practice of a bodhisattva?
Having been liberated from all bonds, having departed from afflictions and shattered Māra, and knowing the mentalities of sentient beings, I pray that you will explain the practice of a bodhisattva.
Like a flower opening its smiling face, you possess the practice that severs existence;
your teaching severs the intent of existence—pray speak of the bodhisattva conduct.
It can bestow immeasurable bliss; it is virtuous merit and virtuous practice.
Throughout all worlds, you bring benefit and peace. Having,
throughout immeasurable lifetimes, renounced all beloved things—
hundreds of elephants, horses, and jewels, as well as countless wives and children.
Having subdued oneself through patience, delighting in the practice of the virtues of the precepts,
and being resolutely diligent in effort, the mind is never troubled by sorrow.
Having exhausted the hundredfold sufferings, that which was sought has reached its ultimate fulfillment.
I pray that you will preach the Dharma as it truly is, to sever and eliminate the suffering of sentient beings.
I pray that you will explain how to be free from the three defilements and how to abandon what is unwholesome.
I pray that you will explain the conduct of Bodhisattvas, who discipline themselves and benefit all living beings.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Abhayacaryā, saying: “Good son,
these ten bodhisattvas previously slandered the Buddha.”
The Bodhisattva Abhayamati said:
“World-Honored One,
how does one slander the Buddha?”
The Buddha said,
“Abhayacārin! In the past,
thirty kalpas ago, there was a buddha named Avalokiteśvara Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who appeared in the world called Jvālā.”

Abhayakumāra! Now, these ten virtuous sons within this assembly shall, after that Tathāgata Avalokiteśvara has entered parinirvāṇa, all become great and wealthy elders of noble lineage; they shall each construct five hundred monasteries, and in each monastery they shall establish one thousand bhikṣus.

At that time, there was a Dharma Master named Bianji (Accumulation of Eloquence) who had attained dhāraṇī. Seated upon the Dharma throne, he preached the Dharma for the assembly; five thousand Buddhas all bestowed eloquence upon him, and eighty trillion devas protected and made offerings to him.

Whenever the Dharma Master Bianji preached the Dharma, seventy thousand sentient beings all attained non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and ten thousand sentient beings attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*.

“Good son! At that time there was a king named Candraprabha (Moon-Attained), who, accompanied by five hundred court ladies, went together to make offerings to the Dharma Master Vāgīśa (Accumulation of Eloquence). Out of reverence for the Dharma, he provided music with songs and scattered various precious flowers over the bhikṣu; he anointed his body with sandalwood and other fragrances, covered him with five hundred fine robes, and for seven days offered all manner of musical instruments and provisions with a devoted heart, honoring him in accordance with the Dharma Master’s own practice.”
"At that time, because that son of a householder spoke ill of that bhikṣu’s violation of the pure precepts,
as retribution for that evil karma, he fell into the great hells for ninety thousand years;
furthermore, for five hundred lifetimes, although born among humans, he took the body of a eunuch, was born among the Mlecchas, and was born into families of wrong views."
For six hundred lifetimes he was born blind and tongueless;
for seven hundred lifetimes, although he left the household life, he sought dhāraṇīs but was unable to obtain them. Why was this?
This is due to the obstruction of evil karma from past lives. "Good son!
You should understand this Dharma gate well; I have now explained it to you."

Having already heard this, if one sees that a Dharma master has indeed broken the precepts, one must not give rise to anger; one should not even speak of it, let alone speak of it after having merely heard of it with the ears.

"Good son! If there were a mass of offenses consisting of plucking out the eyes of all sentient beings, the evil karma of one who looks upon a Dharma teacher with a mind of anger would exceed that mass of offenses."

If one were to commit the entire mass of sin resulting from taking the lives of all sentient beings, and another were to give rise to an evil mind toward a Dharma teacher for even the duration of a single glance or a turning of the face, the former mass of sin would not equal even a hundredth part of this latter mass of sin; it would not equal even a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor an asaṃkhyeya part, nor a kalā part, nor a numerical part, nor even a metaphorical part, up to and including an aupaniṣada part.
Why is this? To slander a Dharma teacher is to slander the Buddha. "Good son!
If there is anyone who wishes to make offerings to the Buddha, that person should instead make offerings to the Dharma Master;
if there is anyone who wishes to provide for the Buddha, that person should instead provide for the Dharma Master;
if there is anyone who wishes to pay homage to the Buddha, that person should instead pay homage to the Dharma Master.
Why is this? Because it is from the Bodhisattva that all-knowledge arises, and it is from the Bodhisattva that all Buddhas arise. "Good son!
What is it for a bodhisattva to be said to "arouse the mind of enlightenment" (bodhicitta)?

Once the mind has been aroused, one should know that one does not dwell in sensual pleasures, is untainted by afflictions, and does not dwell in any non-celibate (abrahmacarya) conduct. It should be understood in this way.
In this way, although the bodhisattva enters the formless concentrations, he is not reborn in the formless realms. Why is this?

The bodhisattva is not born through the power of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), but is born through the power of his vows (*praṇidhāna*). Thus, the bodhisattva liberates all ordinary, foolish worldlings who follow the ways of hair-splitting sophistry.
If there were anyone capable of seeing the color of space, that person would be able to see the afflictions of a bodhisattva. "Good son!

For example, it is like the Nāga King Anavatapta; though he is included among the host of nāgas and his physical form is no different from that of any other nāga, he is entirely free from the three kinds of faults of nāgas."
What are these three?
First, hot sand does not fall upon their heads; second, they do not engage in sexual desire with snake-bodies; third, they have no fear of garuḍas.
In this way, noble son!

Just as these three defects cannot affect the dragon, so too it should be known that the bodhisattva-mahāsattva likewise possesses all forms of play and pleasure, yet the afflictions of desire and the suffering within the three realms of existence cannot obscure him. Thus should it be understood.
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like the species of beings that catch fish; they move within the water, see objects within the water, and enter the water without dying."

Good son! It is the same for the bodhisattva-mahāsattva: though they move within saṃsāra and abide in the conduct of ordinary beings, they constantly seek wise conduct and cultivate the true Dharma. Their minds are not confused or distracted; they cannot be defiled by the affairs of ordinary beings, nor can they be overcome by the sufferings of the three realms of existence. Therefore, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should always protect themselves and must never slander a Dharma teacher.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"If you wish to make offerings to the Buddha, If you wish to pay homage to the Tathāgata, Simply make offerings to the Son of the Buddha; This is the foremost way to honor the Buddha."
I say that one should give robes and alms bowls, as well as places for sitting, reclining, and walking;
such things should be offered to those who have resolved to attain bodhicitta.
In this way one makes offerings to the Buddha, and in this way one makes offerings to the Dharma.
The Buddha is the supreme among the world, for all arise from the Dharma.
This person of solitary wisdom brings light to those with blinded eyes;
he shows the right path to the lost and leads them toward the deathless realm.
Even if one were to constantly offer all manner of wealth and treasures to all Buddhas,
though such offerings be made with devotion, they could not repay the Buddha’s kindness;
yet, if from this day forward one constantly makes offerings to the Dharma Master, [one will repay that kindness].
"One who does not slander and does not speak [of such things] shall repay the kindness of all Buddhas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Abhayacārin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"Is there a skillful means that can cause this bodhisattva to purify his evil karma?
The Buddha said, "There is."
Abhayakumāra! There is a dhāraṇī;
if this son of good family can leave the household life and recite these dhāraṇī phrases with single-minded devotion, his evil karma will be purified.
Tadyathā (the *ā* is a long vowel; where "long" is not explicitly stated, all are short vowels):
*gaṇe*, *gañje*, *gañjapeṭe*, *gañjanaviḷe*, *gañjaśreṣṭhe*, *gañjakalpite*, *gañjayohye*, *ghaṭye*, *abhyahye*.
The long vowel *ā* is a heavy syllable (*guru*), while those not stated as heavy are all light syllables (*laghu*).
*Pa*, *ku*, *tu*, *ru*, *ṭa*, *ga*, *ma*, *yu*, *da*, *ja*, *ta*—these are long vowels. *Na*, *pa*, *ra*, *pha*, *ba*—these are [heavy] syllables.
*Ni*, *ga*, *ti*, *dhi* (pronounced with the *chai* tone), *u*, *ga*, *ra*, *hi*—these are [heavy] syllables. *Hu*, *hu*, *mi* (pronounced with the *wu-yei* tone), *ca*, *pa*.

The verse of beauty, the verse of *sacittamaṇi*, the verse of *samādhi*, the verse of the long vowel *jñā*, the verse of *nayapariśuddhi*, the verse of the long vowel *dīrgha*, and the verse of the heavy syllable *tī*. "O son of good family!..."

If these ten good men can recite these dharani phrases for seven days, relinquishing all else, abstaining from mixed foods, keeping the mind undistracted, not clinging to forms, and not engaging in mental discrimination; if they abandon arrogance, constantly reciting without ceasing and doing nothing else; if they do not mingle with others, practice an impartial mind, and always act for the benefit of others; if their minds constantly cultivate the impermanence of the five aggregates without abandoning them, and they constantly practice mindfulness of the Buddha—if they practice in this manner, they will see a thousand Buddhas appearing before them throughout the ten directions.

At that time, when those ten virtuous sons in the assembly had heard what the Buddha spoke, they immediately left the household life. With single-minded devotion, they recited these dharani phrases; for seven days they practiced with diligence, following and internalizing them, and they also constantly cultivated the buddhānusmṛti-samādhi (the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha). They beheld one thousand Buddhas, and their obstructing karmic hindrances from evil deeds were entirely expiated and extinguished through repentance.

At that time, he immediately attained the *Sarvajñatāmukhasamuccaya-dhāraṇī*, extinguished the karma of birth and death for thirty kalpas, and became non-retrogressive from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Abhaya, you should know that the King Candraprabha who at that time made offerings to the Dharma Master was none other than the present Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Amitāyus."
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Akṣobhya was, at that time, the Dharma Master Vādiprabhūta.

Those ten sons of eminent householders who at that time slandered the Dharma Master Vādiprabhūta are these ten virtuous men in this assembly. Those ten sons of eminent householders who at that time slandered the Dharma Master Vādiprabhūta for violating the pure precepts are these very ones.
"In this way, noble son!

Whatever monastery a bodhisattva may inhabit, whether it be well-established or poorly established, they shall not perceive any fault therein, even at the cost of their life or upon the occasion of death."
Why is this? Good son! A bodhisattva possesses four kinds of pure dharmas.
What are the four kinds?

First, cultivating emptiness; second, never harboring a destructive mind toward any sentient being; third, constantly bestowing benefit upon all bodhisattvas; and fourth, preaching the Dharma without seeking material sustenance.
“Good son! These are the four dharmas that purify the bodhi of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to clarify this meaning, spoke in verse:
"If one can believe and understand emptiness— the supreme dharma taught by the Buddha—
then practicing such pure conduct, one should always be heedful.
One should not harm sentient beings, nor speak words that cause division."
That person shall attain Buddhahood, their radiance illuminating the world.
This is the second path of purity; having heard it, act for the benefit [of others], practice patience toward sentient beings, and do not engage in destructive conduct.
There is a dharma that is wholesome and stainless: when a bodhisattva who has resolved upon awakening gives a gift and does not seek gratitude or reward, this is the third path to enlightenment.
Resolutely giving rise to a compassionate heart, he teaches the Dharma without seeking profit.
"Just as there is deep compassion, so too is the purity of the knowledge of the fourth path.
Furthermore, son of good family!"

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who cultivates dhāraṇīs practices in the forest hermitage (*araṇya*), stays close to hearing the Dharma, wears fresh and clean robes, and dwells alone in seclusion. Amidst the four modes of deportment, he constantly contemplates his practice; he bestows various offerings upon the Dharma Master, gives rise to right faith without following the words of others, and never succumbs to weariness. He always exerts himself with vigor, his mind free from flattery or deceit; he does not abandon the mindfulness of the Buddha, yet his mind remains non-apprehending. He skillfully cultivates signlessness and acts according to what has been taught; with a mind of faith and understanding, he requests the Buddha for repentance, rejoices in merit, and dedicates it toward constant, upright practice. He does not transgress the rules of deportment nor fear admonitions; relying on the noble ones, he abides in all renowned practices, cultivating them within this Dharma without ever becoming weary.
When this Dharma was being taught, thirty thousand sentient beings who had never before resolved to attain bodhicitta did so upon hearing this Dharma;
five thousand sentient beings became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena;
and thirty thousand bodhisattvas all attained the forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
“Good son! If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas hear this Dharma-gate, they will obtain exceedingly great merit.

Suppose one were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and offer them to the Triple Gem every single day, continuing in this manner for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges; [the merit of hearing this Dharma-gate would still surpass it].”
If one further hears such a Dharma-gate, their merit shall be superior.
Even if one were able to practice the five *pāramitās* for a thousand kalpas, excluding only the gateway of the *prajñāpāramitā*;
if a person hears such a Dharma-gate, their merit shall be superior.
“Good son! If there were someone who, for a thousand Buddhas, rose at dawn, during the day, and at dusk to make offerings, to honor and praise them, and to provide for their every need;
yet if another were to hear such a Dharma-gate as this, the latter’s merit would be superior.”
"In this way, noble son!

You should protect and keep this Dharma-gate in mind. I now entrust it to you so that you may guard, uphold, read, recite, explain its meaning, and cause it to be written down; even at the cost of your life or death, you should protect and keep it in mind, practicing in accordance with it."

When the Tathāgata had finished speaking thus, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Abhayacintin and the other bodhisattvas, all those bhikṣus and the entire assembly, together with the devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly filled with joy.
Slandering the Buddha's sutras
